title: Lessons from Studying Every Memory System — Shlok Khemani, Independent
talk_summary: Shlok Khemani reverse-engineered how ChatGPT and Claude implement personalization memory, tracing their convergence on a periodically-updated 'running profile' plus on-demand conversation search tools. The core lessons are that memory must be built in-house and tuned to your product, that profile length and update frequency are explicit compute trade-offs, and that stale/conflicting memories persist because products don't detect or resolve conflicts.

takeaways.technique: Running profile with periodic async synthesis ('dreaming')
takeaways.what_they_do: Every 24h (Claude) or few days (ChatGPT), an LLM reads recent conversations and rewrites a compact profile that is injected into every new context, instead of per-fact lists or pure RAG.
takeaways.numbers: ChatGPT profile ~4,000 tokens updated every few days; Claude ~1,000 tokens updated every 24 hours

takeaways.technique: Dense keyword-clue memories vs. verbose sentences as a token trade-off
takeaways.what_they_do: ChatGPT packs memories as dense keyword clues relying on model inference; Claude uses full sentences but a smaller profile — an explicit serving-cost vs. update-cost trade-off.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they're trying to put in keywords almost like clues and because LLM especially the frontier models today are so good at inferring context

takeaways.technique: On-demand retrieval tools over history instead of always-injected context
takeaways.what_they_do: Claude V1 gave the model tools to search past conversations by keyword/topic and by time period, starting each session fresh and retrieving only when needed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the model was given two tools. It was given a tool to search over previous conversations by keyword or topic

takeaways.technique: Conflict detection and staleness flagging in stored memory
takeaways.what_they_do: The speaker's main critique: profiles keep stale or contradictory facts (e.g. a trip never taken) and never notice the conflict; he argues detecting gaps is a product problem, not a model limitation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what really bothers me is that chat GPD today doesn't realize that there is a conflict. It's not curious about trying to fill in gaps

takeaways.technique: Don't outsource memory; co-design it with the workflow
takeaways.what_they_do: Observed that every top consumer product builds memory in-house because implementations differ per product; off-the-shelf memory is an afterthought that doesn't fit.
takeaways.evidence_quote: memory cannot be outsourced. If you're a serious team, you do not outsource memory. It is something that you build alongside your product
